Getting this right determines media allocation, and the honest version of the analysis is a first-stage moderated mediation: the campaign is randomized, so the differential effect on the awareness measure across segments is identified, while the awareness-to-purchase slope is not. The [uplift modeling](#sec-uplift-modeling) chapter treats the targeting problem directly, and the conditional process model is best read as supplying the mechanistic story behind an uplift ranking rather than as a competing estimator.

In platform and operations settings, the moderator is often a system state rather than a person: network congestion, inventory depth, marketplace thickness. Here the moderator sometimes *is* manipulable, because the platform sets it, and the interaction framing becomes legitimate. A two-factor experiment that randomizes both the intervention and the system state converts a fragile effect-modification claim into a genuine causal interaction, and makes the mediated-moderation decomposition of Section \@ref(sec-cpa-mediated-moderation) well posed. This is usually worth the extra design cost.

In litigation and regulatory work, moderated mediation claims attract scrutiny precisely at their weakest point. An expert who testifies that a disclosure worked through comprehension for sophisticated investors but not for retail investors is making a claim about a difference between two indirect effects, and opposing counsel will ask whether that difference was tested. On the evidence in Section \@ref(sec-cpa-probing), the answer in most submitted analyses is no. The defensible version reports the index with its interval, states the mediator-outcome confounding assumption explicitly, and presents the sensitivity analysis alongside the point estimate.

In policy evaluation, the analogue is heterogeneity of mechanism across sites. Multi-site trials routinely find that a program works everywhere but appears to work through different channels in different places. Before that becomes an implementation recommendation it needs the index test, because site sample sizes vary enormously and the differential-significance artifact of Section \@ref(sec-cpa-probing) is precisely a sample-size artifact.

## Summary {#sec-cpa-summary}

Moderated mediation asks whether a mechanism is contingent, and conditional process analysis is the family of models that answers it. The conditional indirect effect is the product of the conditional first-stage and second-stage paths, which makes it linear in the moderator only when exactly one stage is moderated; in that case its slope is the index of moderated mediation, and testing the index is the correct test. Mediated moderation, under the standard linear specification, computes the same number from the other direction, and the term has been retired because an interaction product is not a manipulable cause outside a factorial design.

The dominant reporting practice, probing the indirect effect at conventional moderator values and comparing which intervals exclude zero, is not a test and behaves very badly: in a simulation where the true index is zero and the only difference between groups is sample size, it claims moderated mediation three quarters of the time. The index test holds its nominal level.

Counterfactually, most applied moderation of a mechanism is effect modification rather than interaction, which is both weaker and easier: it needs no assumption about the moderator's own confounding, but it licenses no statement about changing the moderator. First-stage moderated mediation is the credible case, because a randomized treatment identifies the interaction that drives it, and @loeys2016assessing show that this makes moderated mediation identifiable under weaker assumptions than mediation itself. Second-stage moderation carries the full burden of mediator-outcome confounding and no differencing argument relieves it.

The replication of @brader2008triggers shows the whole apparatus at work and delivers a result worth keeping: the framing treatment operates through anxiety at every age, the mechanism does not measurably vary with age, and what does vary with age is the direct path that bypasses anxiety entirely. A causal forest reaches the same conclusion without being told to look at age. The power simulation explains why: detecting moderated mediation takes roughly four times the sample that detecting mediation takes, and most published conditional process analyses are not built at that scale.

Outside the laboratory the order of operations matters more than the model. @singh2026profitability is the template: establish the total effect with a design that survives estimators with different failure modes, build the mediator and the moderator from data granular enough that a threshold means something, and then decompose, stating plainly which parts of the decomposition are design based and which rest on selection on observables.

Some mechanism claims do not fit a regression at all. When the theory says that several distinct combinations of conditions reach the same outcome, that one condition is present in all of them, and that the conditions for failure are not the mirror image of the conditions for success, the set-theoretic tools are the right ones. Configurational analysis expresses equifinality, conjunctural causation, and asymmetry natively, at the cost of giving up standard errors and inheriting every confounder in the sample. It characterizes heterogeneity; it does not identify effects. Used alongside a credible design rather than in place of one, it answers the question a coefficient cannot: not how large the average effect is, but in which configurations the mechanism operates at all.
